I’m coming up on one year into a 25 Year personal Trading Experiment.

The goal is simple: to transparently compare active swing trading with long-term investing in a global index fund, and to see how both approaches hold up over time.

So far this year, the swing trading account is up 14.9%, which currently puts it 8.7% ahead of the global index. I’m very aware that one year means very little in market terms, and that luck, market regime, and timing all play a role. I’m not drawing any big conclusions yet.

This experiment is intended to run for 25 years, with 24 years still ahead. Whether it is actually possible to outperform the market consistently over such a long period is an open question. I am not claiming to have the answer, only a willingness to test it honestly and in public.

To keep myself accountable, I share trades transparently: entries, position sizing, risk, stops, targets, and performance over time. Some years may look good, others likely will not, and there is a real chance this looks naive in hindsight. That uncertainty is part of the process.

If this kind of long-term, transparent approach to trading and investing is of interest, feel free to follow along. I also share everything on my website and through a free trading dashboard where current positions and performance are visible.

Hopefully this is useful, or at least an honest data point, for your own trading or investing journey.

🧰 Expressing a Swing Trade: Equity vs Bull Call Spreads

There are many ways to express a swing trade in the market. The most common, and often the first, is simply buying shares and managing risk with a stop-loss.

As traders evolve, questions around capital efficiency, risk definition, and portfolio construction naturally arise. This is often where options enter the conversation.

In this thread, I’ll walk through one specific swing trade on $TGT and compare two ways of expressing the same trade idea, without changing the thesis.

The trade idea is a higher-timeframe bullish reversal on $TGT.

The setup is based on weekly and monthly market structure, liquidity taken below prior monthly lows and the Covid low, and a clear upside target into an untested bearish Order Block.

Key levels used for both structures:
• Entry: ~$99.55
• Stop: ~$83.44
• Target: ~$125'

This is not a day or intraday trade. It is a high-conviction swing designed to give price room to work.

🧰 Expressing a Swing Trade: Equity vs Bull Call Spreads

There are many ways to express a swing trade in the market. The most common, and often the first, is simply buying shares and managing risk with a stop-loss.

As traders evolve, questions around capital efficiency, risk definition, and portfolio construction naturally arise. This is often where options enter the conversation.

In this thread, I’ll walk through one specific swing trade on $TGT and compare two ways of expressing the same trade idea, without changing the thesis.

text:
Option 1 is the equity swing trade.

For comparison purposes, the position is sized so that the dollar risk is approximately $1,000, using the same entry and stop-loss levels.

This results in buying roughly 62 shares, with about $6,200 of capital deployed. Risk is defined by the stop-loss, and reward is realized if price reaches the predefined target.

Equity works well because there is no time constraint, no time decay, and price can move slowly without invalidating the trade.

The trade-off with equity is capital usage and gap risk.

A relatively large amount of capital is committed relative to the defined risk, and losses can exceed the planned stop in the event of a large opening gap.

Equity trades are robust and intuitive, but capital-heavy.

text:
Option 2 is a long-dated Bull Call Spread.

Instead of buying shares, the trade is expressed by buying a call near current price and selling a call at the predefined target, using a long-dated expiry to reduce time pressure.

This structure fits naturally with the trade plan, as the exit level is already defined in advance.

For the 12-month Bull Call Spread on $TGT

• Buy the 95 Call
• Sell the 125 Call
• Expiry: ~12 months
Capital at risk is approximately $1,185 and is fully defined at entry. The maximum profit is about $1,700, resulting in a slightly lower risk-to-reward compared to equity.
The primary benefit here is capital efficiency and risk definition, not higher expectancy.

text:
Equity and long-dated Bull Call Spreads are not competing ideas. They are tools designed for different constraints.

Equity excels when time is not a binding variable and risk is scaled through position sizing. Long-dated Bull Call Spreads excel when capital efficiency and defined risk matter, and when time risk must be managed rather than ignored.

For this $TGT setup, the thesis does not change. Only the risk container and time exposure do.
